en: Kanchoro Khan or Kyyaz Khan!
If only these men came near,
These villains who ravaged the people,
I would seize one and rip open his belly,
And swallow the black blood within
To quench my thirst.
If only I could tear one apart and slaughter him,
Drink his blood like kumiss,
And glut myself upon it;
Then my burning heart might be soothed,
My dimmed eyes might open,
All my anguish might scatter,
And my brow brighten like a mirror—
That would fulfill my desire.
If only I could bring greater havoc
Upon Kanchoro Khan and Kyyaz!”
So thought the warrior woman Aichürök,
That extraordinary, wrathful woman.
But the thought came to her too late:
If she met them, she would take their heads,
Bring grievous misery upon them,
Strike when they came near,
Count their vile lives as nothing,
And sever their heads with her sword.
Even if it meant her death,
Dear sister-in-law had reached
A resolve from which she would not retreat.
She was ready to fight them to the death;
The poor woman braced herself
To sacrifice her fly-like soul.
When she saw the tyrant khans,
The indomitable woman Aichürök
Coiled like a striking snake,
But there were no Argyn or Kyrgyz warriors
To break through and rescue her.
Your sister-in-law contemplated true battle,
But many wrestlers surrounded her.
Alone and suffering,
This woman bore endless sorrow;
Many champions encircled her.
Your heroic sister-in-law Aichürök
Was about to unleash a mighty conflict.
She spoke softly, yet firmly,
The moon-faced lady, in anguish,
And to brave Kyyaz and Kanchoro,
To those two she began to speak:
“Panther born of a mongrel,
Brave Kyyaz, born of a raven,
How can I take you as my ‘companion’?
How can I overcome my grief,
How can I lie beside a wastrel?
Panther born of a falcon,
Brave Kyyaz, born of a crow,
How can I bare my breast?
How can I share his bed?
This Kyyaz who struck you from above—
Is it right that he should take
The bed of the noble gray-maned hero,
Or that he should rise after striking from above?
And is it right that he should take
The pillow of the gray-maned hero?
Or rise after striking from beside him?
The two reins and the single lead—
How can I take them in my hands?
Without suffering disgrace, calamity, and strife,
How can I go to the Jediger?
After my magnanimous lord, great as Ala-Too,
How can I remain alive?
Hearing endless gossip among the people,
The pampered lady Chachykey
Will hear that I took Kanchoro,
Her heart will surge with grief,
And tears will stream from her eyes.
In her old age, Kanykey
Has been sustained by Aichürök,
Who has watched over her,
And sheltered the child left behind,
Keeping him beneath her protection,
Though her lovely face was wounded.
Her valor flared, her eyes flashed,
And the lone woman’s sorrow boiled.
Then Aichürök
Said this to Khan Kyyaz,
Telling him of dreadful calamity;
When she began, she spoke thus:
“Such words are unknown among kin.”
Then she addressed Kanchoro,
Her blood boiling as she stood,
Ready to spring like a white lion,
With no dear kinsman left,
And said this to Kanchoro:
“Upon Buurul, who would not yield when asked,
My choro, you cast your cold lasso.
His beloved Chürök, who would not yield to entreaty,
You have taken as plunder;
You have turned against your own kin,
Murdered your own uncle,
And, choro, become monstrous beyond all others!
You began a campaign against your elder brother,
And left sixty noble widows
To make the village desolate.
My choro, you brought misery upon your lord;
You left the few Kyrgyz of mighty Ala-Too
And your homeland desolate!
My choro, Jylgyn, Keng-Kol,
And broad Talas—
You have left your lands desolate;
The prosperous Kyrgyz and the few Argyn—
You have left your people desolate.
Now who but he will whet
Black-edged Zulpukor till it bites?
If the countless Argyn and many Kyrgyz
Are surrounded and fired upon by the infidel,
Who will lead them out of battle?
Who but he will whet
The daring, mighty Zulpukor?
If countless surging foes arise,
If enemies overrun Ala-Too,
Who will rally and lead
This people standing forlorn?
You killed your mountain-like uncle
And fled beyond the pass;
You have not a knucklebone’s worth of sense.
You cast the great Kyrgyz nation,
A people with a royal encampment, into hell,
And were swept away in the flood!
Think what turmoil this will bring—
With six swift horses,
And a letter small as a palm,
Over rugged hills and passes,
Across deserts no man treads,
By night, though it be dark,
If word reaches your people in Dyngsha
That a choro has become a murderer,
And the report travels this far—
To the bloodline of Kaldai,
To the city of Kakan,
And to every living people
Whose ears hear and eyes see—
Will not the khan ride out upon the road,
And the land fill with his army?
Will not bows thunder and tumult rise,
And royal blood be shed?
When the great host comes roaring,
My Kanchoro, will they not slaughter you?
Will they not cast your band into hell,
And massacre them without restraint?
If myriad enemies come to war,
Their poison burning in the quiver,
Brave Kyyaz, khan of the Jediger,
Will meet his doom together with you.
You dog-born, bootlicking slave,
You truly have no sense!
China lies on your left,
Russia lies on your right;
They have guns to confront you,
And many enemies contend with you.
They will raid your villages from Talas;
The Kakan people you challenged
Will destroy every trace of you,
Seize your mares as booty,
Smash your brains across the ground,
And vent their every spite upon you.
They will ignore your pleas;
May you burn, glowing like an ember,
You fawning madman—
May God give you your due!
While my magnanimous lord lived,
You turned my gold to charcoal;
Once fattened, you ruined the village.
You turned my silver to charcoal;
Once fattened, you set all ablaze.
While my prince, vast as the sea, lived,
Did you seize and devour your equal?
You depraved madman,
When the hour of combat came,
Did you think yourself his equal kinsman?”
Burning with fury, Aichürök
Raged and gathered force,
Denouncing Kanchoro;
She began a grave, instructive speech
And lashed him with words like these.
Upon her proud head,
Beside her wretched mother Kanykey,
Her bloodied face was torn,
And her precious hair, long as meadow grass,
Spread across her breast.
Before anyone could utter a word,
In the blink of an eye,
Looking neither up nor down,
Not sparing her life from death,
The hapless woman began the slaughter.
Parted from her mighty lion,
She bound her dog-born, wretched life
To a single strand of hair.
Semetey’s Aichürök
Plunged into the fray,
And entered a mighty conflict
From which there could be no healing.
Among Kyyaz’s Jediger
Stood countless warriors prepared;
Yet the mourning woman Aichürök
Unleashed, as you see, a mighty battle,
With swiftness beyond measure.
In one lightning movement, the ill-fated woman
Drew the sword from its sheath.
She charged like a lion,
As if wisdom came from the unseen;
Her eyes flashed in fury,
And a terrible blood-drinking look seized her,
As she bit her lips and ground her teeth.
With swiftness beyond measure,
The ill-fated woman, blade ringing,
Took the monstrous steel Zulpukor
And gripped it properly;
She sprang like a striking snake,
About to cut Kanchoro down.
As she drew the sword across
And was about to deliver the mighty blow,
To strike the crooked, faithless
Scoundrel across the throat,
And put the raging madman
To death,
The mourning woman Aichürök,
Who had begun a true bloodletting,
Was surrounded by many warriors
Of that infidel Kanchoro.
Just as she was about to strike,
And knock off his apple-like head,
The warriors came between them.
Ejibay, son of Emil,
Was an ungainly wrestler;
And beside the black-tongued, fleet-footed
Slave Kanchoro
Was a wrestler called Töö Balban.
Ejibay and Töö Balban—
Those two blocked her path.
She was a man-killing, fearsome woman:
Not merely two, but seven of them
She beheaded with her sword.
God forbid that one should see it—
The palace filled with dust,
And the gateway ran with blood.
Aichürök moved like a whirlwind;
The warriors who pressed in,
Those who obeyed the khan’s command
And dared oppose Chürök,
Fell sprawling to the ground.
Warriors who fancied themselves skillful
Fell stiffly to the ground,
Their bodies without heads.
The widowed Aichürök,
When Jylgyn and Talas lay in turmoil,
When the royal camp was being plundered—
The widowed Aichürök
Made her proud head her banner,
